content: Glimepiride exhibits no significant pharmacokinetic differences between healthy individuals and patients with type 2 diabetes. The drug's clearance remains consistent across the dose range of 1 mg to 8 mg, demonstrating linear pharmacokinetics. In healthy individuals, intra-individual variability in glimepiride pharmacokinetic parameters ranges from 15% to 23%, while inter-individual variability ranges from 24% to 29%. Metabolism: Glimepiride undergoes complete oxidative biotransformation following either oral or intravenous administration. The primary metabolites are the cyclohexyl hydroxy methyl derivative (M1) and the carboxyl derivative (M2). The conversion of glimepiride to M1 is mediated by the cytochrome P450 2C9 enzyme. M1 is further metabolized to M2 by one or more cytosolic enzymes. M2 is pharmacologically inactive. In animal studies, M1 retains approximately one-third of the pharmacological activity of glimepiride, but its clinical significance in humans regarding blood glucose control remains uncertain. Excretion: When orally administered radiolabeled glimepiride (14C-glimepiride) was given to three healthy male subjects, approximately 60% of the total radioactivity was recovered in the urine within seven days. M1 and M2 accounted for 80% to 90% of the radioactivity in the urine, with the M1-to-M2 ratio being approximately 3:2 in two subjects and 4:1 in one subject. About 40% of the total radioactivity was recovered in feces, with M1 and M2 accounting for approximately 70% of the radioactivity (M1-to-M2 ratio of 1:3). No parent drug was detected in either urine or feces. After intravenous administration in patients, no significant biliary excretion of glimepiride or its M1 metabolite was observed. Geriatric Patients: A multiple-dose study compared glimepiride pharmacokinetics in type 2 diabetes patients aged ≤65 years and >65 years, using a daily dose of 6 mg. No significant differences in pharmacokinetics were observed between the two age groups. The mean area under the curve (AUC) at steady state was approximately 13% lower in older patients, while the mean weight-adjusted clearance was about 11% higher in older patients compared to younger ones. Gender: No differences in glimepiride pharmacokinetics were observed between males and females when adjusted for body weight differences. Race: No specific studies have been conducted to evaluate the effects of race on glimepiride pharmacokinetics. However, in placebo-controlled trials involving patients with type 2 diabetes, reductions in HbA1c were comparable among Caucasians, Blacks, and Hispanics. Renal Impairment: In a single-dose, open-label study, 3 mg of glimepiride was administered to patients with varying degrees of renal impairment, categorized by creatinine clearance (CLcr): Group I: Mild impairment (CLcr >50 mL/min) Group II: Moderate impairment (CLcr 20–50 mL/min) Group III: Severe impairment (CLcr <20 mL/min) The mean AUC for M2 was six times higher in Group III compared to Group I. The apparent terminal half-life (T1/2) of glimepiride remained unchanged, but the half-lives of M1 and M2 increased as renal function declined. Hepatic Impairment: The effect of hepatic impairment on glimepiride pharmacokinetics is unknown, as no adequate studies have been conducted in this population. Obese Patients: In a single-dose study involving 28 type 2 diabetes patients with either normal body weight or morbid obesity, the pharmacokinetics of glimepiride and its metabolites were assessed. Tmax, clearance, and volume of distribution were similar between the two groups. However, morbidly obese patients exhibited lower Cmax and AUC values compared to those with normal body weight. The mean Cmax, AUC0-24, and AUC0-∞ values for glimepiride in normal-weight versus morbidly obese patients were 547 ± 218 ng/mL vs. 410 ± 124 ng/mL, 3210 ± 1030 hours·ng/mL vs. 2820 ± 1110 hours·ng/mL, and 4000 ± 1320 hours·ng/mL vs. 3280 ± 1360 hours·ng/mL, respectively. Drug Interactions: Aspirin: In a randomized, double-blind, two-period, crossover study, healthy subjects received either placebo or aspirin (1 gram three times daily) for five days. On the fourth day of each study period, a single 1 mg dose of glimepiride was administered. The glimepiride doses were separated by a 14-day washout period. Co-administration of aspirin resulted in a 34% decrease in the mean glimepiride AUC and a 4% decrease in the mean glimepiride Cmax.
